utilities.name: PG&E
utilities.rate_note: Illustrative blended residential ballpark for high-usage PG&E homes after recent rate cycles — verify with your bill and rate schedule (E-TOU, EV2-A, etc.).
utilities.headline: Is solar worth it on a PG&E bill?
utilities.summary: PG&E customers often start solar research after a summer bill spike — not because they love panels. Model payback with your rate and roof, then compare quotes without trusting a salesperson’s black-box savings claim.

sections.heading: Why PG&E bills push people to research solar
sections.body: Homeowners in PG&E territory usually open a solar tab after a concrete month — a July/August bill, a rate notice, or a neighbor’s install. Past behavior looks the same: two installer websites, one “free savings estimate,” then stalled confusion because every quote assumes a different rate and system size. Your decision is less about whether solar “works in California” and more about whether the numbers on your bill and roof match the pitch.

sections.heading: Net Billing vs. the savings story you’ll hear
sections.body: California’s Net Billing Tariff credits exports differently than classic NEM. Export-heavy designs can look worse on paper than self-consumption + battery. When you decode a quote, ask what export credit and self-consumption assumptions they used — and whether battery is required for their savings claim. SolarFlow separates bill offset from backup so you can see both jobs clearly.

sections.heading: What to do before the sales appointment
sections.body: Pull your last 12 months of usage if you have them, note your rate schedule from the bill, and model your address with Google Solar roof data. That gives you a spouse-ready baseline before anyone asks for a deposit. Also skim local permit timelines so soft costs don’t ambush you after you say yes.

faqs.question: What rate should I use for a PG&E solar ROI model?
faqs.answer: Use your blended effective rate from recent bills (total $ ÷ kWh), not a marketing “average California rate.” Time-of-use schedules change the $/kWh you avoid. SolarFlow lets you enter bill, usage, and $/kWh so they stay in sync.

faqs.question: Do I need a battery with solar on PG&E?
faqs.answer: Not always, but Net Billing often makes self-consumption and evening use more important. Batteries also matter for wildfire / PSPS backup — a different job than bill savings. Toggle battery in the ROI model to compare both paths.

faqs.question: How do I know if a PG&E-area solar quote is fair?
faqs.answer: Normalize to dollars per watt before incentives, system size (kW), and whether battery is included. Then run our free quote market check and compare against your address-level model — not against another installer’s spreadsheet.

utilities.name: SCE
utilities.rate_note: Illustrative blended residential ballpark — confirm from your SCE bill and schedule.
utilities.headline: Solar bill calculator thinking for SCE customers
utilities.summary: If your Southern California Edison bill jumped and you’re comparing quotes, start with your roof and rate — not county averages. Build a neutral model you can share with a spouse before you sit through a pitch.

sections.heading: Bill shock is the real trigger
sections.body: SCE customers rarely “decide to go green” in the abstract. They react to a bill, a heat wave, or a rate change, then collect quotes that disagree with each other. The pain is distrust: different kW sizes, different assumed rates, and savings graphs nobody can audit.

sections.heading: Net Billing still applies
sections.body: Like other California IOUs, export credits under Net Billing are not 1:1 retail. Ask every quote to break out self-consumed kWh vs. exported kWh. If they won’t, treat the savings number as soft.

sections.heading: Permits and HOAs kill momentum
sections.body: Many SCE-area deals stall after a quote when HOA architectural review or city fire setbacks appear. Check process reality for your ZIP before you emotionally commit — SolarFlow’s permit tools and local guides help surface those steps early.

faqs.question: Is solar worth it with SCE rates?
faqs.answer: It depends on your usage, roof production, and rate schedule — not a statewide slogan. Model your address, then pressure-test installer quotes against that baseline.

faqs.question: What should I bring to an SCE solar appointment?
faqs.answer: Recent bills (or usage chart), your roof readiness notes, and a short list of questions about $/W, warranties, and Net Billing assumptions. A shareable SolarFlow report helps keep the conversation specific.

utilities.name: SDG&E
utilities.rate_note: SDG&E often ranks among the highest U.S. residential rates; this is an illustrative blend — use your bill.
utilities.headline: High SDG&E bills and whether solar pays back
utilities.summary: San Diego–area homeowners search solar because rates hurt. Get an address-level model with transparent assumptions so you can compare quotes without another high-pressure appointment.

sections.heading: High rates change the math — if the quote is honest
sections.body: Elevated $/kWh improves payback when you displace your own usage. It does not fix a bad roof, bad pricing, or opaque financing. Your job is to separate rate-driven opportunity from salesperson optimism.

sections.heading: Coast vs inland production
sections.body: San Diego County roofs vary — marine layer, orientation, and shade matter. Google Solar–based layouts beat hand-wavy “homes in your ZIP save $X” claims.

sections.heading: Compare quotes like a buyer, not a lead
sections.body: Normalize each proposal to $/W, equipment brands, battery inclusion, and timeline to PTO. Use the quote market-check tool, then share one spouse-ready PDF so decisions happen in your kitchen, not on a driveway pitch.

faqs.question: Why are solar quotes in San Diego all over the map?
faqs.answer: Different system sizes, battery packages, financing (loan vs cash), and Net Billing assumptions. Always convert to cash $/W and model your roof separately.

utilities.name: Con Edison
utilities.rate_note: Illustrative NYC-area residential blend — delivery + supply vary; confirm on your Con Edison bill.
utilities.headline: Solar on a Con Edison bill: what to model first
utilities.summary: NYC-area bills stack supply and delivery. Before you chase a rooftop or community-solar sales call, understand your usage and whether your building/roof can host a system at all.

sections.heading: Dense housing changes the job
sections.body: Many Con Edison customers hit co-op boards, roof rights, or shading from neighboring buildings. Feasibility and process pain show up before ROI spreadsheets do. Start with roof readiness, then economics.

sections.heading: Incentives change — don’t memorize last year’s ad
sections.body: Federal credits and state/NYSERDA-era programs evolve. Ask for current eligibility in writing and keep a neutral model so you’re not dependent on a flyer.

faqs.question: Can apartment dwellers use SolarFlow?
faqs.answer: SolarFlow models rooftop systems at an address. If you lack roof rights, community solar or other products may fit better — still start by understanding your bill and usage.

utilities.name: Duke Energy
utilities.rate_note: Illustrative — Duke territories differ by state; always use your bill’s effective rate.
utilities.headline: Solar with Duke Energy: bill math without the pitch
utilities.summary: Lower average rates than coastal California mean payback hinges on system cost, production, and incentives. Model your address so a low $/kWh doesn’t get buried under an aggressive loan payment.

sections.heading: When rates are moderate, price discipline matters more
sections.body: If you’re not escaping 40¢/kWh bills, an overpriced system takes longer to break even. Quote comparison and $/W checks matter even more than in high-rate utilities.

sections.heading: Interconnection still has a process
sections.body: Utility interconnection and local building permits still gate Permission to Operate. Know the steps so timeline surprises don’t erode trust after you sign.

faqs.question: Is solar worth it if my Duke rate is “only” 12–16¢/kWh?
faqs.answer: Possibly — especially with incentives, rising rates, or long ownership horizon — but the margin for quote padding is thinner. Run the numbers with your roof and compare installed $/W carefully.

utilities.name: FPL
utilities.rate_note: Illustrative residential blend — Florida rates and net metering rules vary; verify locally.
utilities.headline: FPL bills, Florida sun, and realistic solar payback
utilities.summary: Florida has strong sun and frequent sales pressure. Anchor on your roof production and all-in system cost before you accept a “$0 down” payment that hides the economics.

sections.heading: Sunlight is not the same as a good deal
sections.body: Great irradiance helps production; it does not justify every financed package. Homeowners who get stuck usually skipped normalizing quotes to cash economics.

sections.heading: Hurricane and roof age questions
sections.body: Ask about roof condition, mounting, and warranty interactions with storm risk. Production models assume the array stays installed and performing.

faqs.question: Should I replace my roof before solar in Florida?
faqs.answer: If the roof is near end of life, installers often recommend reroofing first. Factor that cost into true payback — SolarFlow’s planning tools help you keep assumptions visible.

utilities.name: APS
utilities.rate_note: Illustrative — desert TOU and demand components vary; pull numbers from your APS bill.
utilities.headline: APS + Arizona sun: model before you buy
utilities.summary: Phoenix-area roofs produce strong output, but rate design (TOU, demand) shapes savings. Enter your real bill and usage so a quote can’t hide behind “Arizona averages.”

sections.heading: TOU and demand change the savings story
sections.body: Ask which rate schedule the quote assumes after solar. A model that ignores demand charges or TOU shifts can overstate monthly savings.

sections.heading: Heat, HVAC, and system sizing
sections.body: High AC load is often why people look at solar. If you’re also considering heat-pump HVAC later, SolarFlow’s toggles help you see stacked scenarios.

faqs.question: Is a battery worth it with APS?
faqs.answer: Backup and rate arbitrage are different jobs. Toggle battery in the ROI dashboard and decide based on outages and your rate — not a bundled “package discount” alone.

utilities.name: Xcel Energy
utilities.rate_note: Illustrative Colorado-oriented blend — Xcel territories differ; use your bill.
utilities.headline: Xcel Energy solar: payback without county averages
utilities.summary: Front Range homeowners often hear conflicting stories about net metering and incentives. Build an address-level baseline, then pressure-test installer math.

sections.heading: Snow, orientation, and production honesty
sections.body: Ask how the proposal handles winter production and roof pitch. Google Solar insights plus a clear production figure beat vague “offset 100% of your bill” language.

sections.heading: Get the assumptions in writing
sections.body: Export or share a SolarFlow report with rate, inflation, system size, and ITC assumptions labeled. That document is what spouses and skeptical partners actually need.

faqs.question: How do I compare Xcel solar quotes quickly?
faqs.answer: Convert to $/W, confirm battery inclusion, and check whether savings use your bill’s rate. Our quote checker flags quotes that sit far above planning benchmarks.
